Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Many journalists, politicians, and creators in India are facing similar issues; accounts being suspended, posts removed, or visibility reduced with little transparency or meaningful recourse.

These actions often happen under two parallel mechanisms of India’s Information Technology Act, 2000.

Section 69A allows the Government to issue blocking orders on broad grounds such as national security or public order. However, these orders are usually confidential, and affected users often receive neither notice nor a copy of the blocking order, making it difficult to challenge them.

Separately, Section 79(3)(b) allows authorities to pressure platforms to remove content by threatening loss of “safe harbour” protections if platforms fail to comply with government or court directions. In practice, this creates strong incentives for platforms to over-comply.

The lack of transparency around these processes raises serious concerns for due process, free expression, and accountability.

Earlier today, @Meta temporarily removed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's video on the NEET paper leaks in India. According to media reports, a Meta spokesperson stated that the post was taken down due to an error and it had since been restored, post-haste.

The temporary removal of PM Modi's post highlights the larger issue of wrongful content takedowns by these platforms, often without any notice to users and leaving them with no meaningful recourse. These takedowns may be carried out by automated systems that have  been deployed as part of the growing due diligence obligations under Rule 3 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, or by way of government-issued order which reflects as a “legal request” on the platform.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has seen multiple instances of automated monitoring systems wrongfully taking down content, with no available recourse but engaging with the platform's internal appeals mechanisms and grievance officers. While high profile instances such as this are resolved quickly, ordinary users are often left high and dry. These issues are exacerbated by the lack of human review in the escalation process, with aggrieved users facing constant automated and AI generated responses which often fail to address even the most apparent errors in moderation. Coupled with unresponsive and inefficient grievance officer reporting procedures, users are all but helpless. Platforms may deploy these automated systems to deal with the huge volumes of content that they have to moderate under the existing regulatory system, especially since many of these obligations are tied to the safe harbour provisions under the IT Act that exempt platforms from being liable for the content they host. However, having humans in the loop for grievance redressal would ensure that fair outcomes are delivered to all and not only to high-profile persons.

According to media reports, the Delhi Police has also identified around 450 social media accounts that allegedly shared deepfakes and AI generated content related to the protests. The Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove this kind of content shared during the CJP protests, along with other content considered "objectionable" that relates to the Prime Minister.

Such vague orders that invoke generic grounds such as “objectionable” or “offensive” are inconsistent with the safeguards laid down in Shreya Singhal. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. In the present case, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

The opacity surrounding the reasons for these takedowns goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009. Instead, what we see emerging through these takedowns is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where various government and law enforcement bodies decide the limits of free speech without transparency or oversight. An illustrative example is the temporary restriction faced by the @Cockroachisback’s primary Instagram handle, which was entirely blocked  on the evening of July 22. As per media reports, the account was restored after the Union Government reversed the blocking and advised the law enforcement agency that “action should be limited to specific posts or URLs instead of the entire account.”

It is not just the Prime Minister’s  post or CJP’s account that has faced such removals recently. Under the decentralised and opaque content removal regime, dozens of Instagram posts and videos related to the protests have been taken down, either by automated systems or in response to government orders, and many users have even had their accounts restricted. For these users, without high-profile attention, regaining access to their accounts or having the content restored is a long and arduous process, with no guarantee of remedy or reprieve.

Indian Data Center Legal Investigation Series : Part 1

Data Centers are "critical infrastructure"? Does this statement has legal force?

Here is the full legal investigation of both — this is the core of "No Law" argument.

1. GAZETTE NOTIFICATION 11 OCT 2022 — Infrastructure Tag

What it is:
F. No. 13/1/2017-INF — Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance. Updates Harmonized Master List of Infrastructure Sub-sectors [first created in 2013, updated 2021].

Line inserted: “Data Centre is included in the category of 'Communication' with footnote — Data Centre housed in a dedicated/centralized building for storage and processing of digital data applications with a minimum capacity of 5 MW of IT load”

Statutory Legal Force — VERY LIMITED:

- This is NOT an Act of Parliament. It's an executive notification under executive power.
- Parent authority? No Act defines Harmonized Master List. It's an internal MoF classification for lending.
- What it actually does: Allows data center companies to get easier institutional credit at lower rates, attract foreign investments, ECB eligibility, longer tenure loans, lower risk weights for banks. That's it.

- What it DOES NOT do:
    - Does NOT give power to acquire land
    - Does NOT exempt from Environment Protection Act, 1986 / EIA Notification 2006
    - Does NOT exempt from Forest Conservation Act, Wildlife Protection Act near Kambalakonda
    - Does NOT give right to use water, power, or process citizens' data
    - Does NOT create liability, accountability, transparency 

So legally: It's a banking classification tag, not a data center governance law. You can get cheap loan, but you still need all other laws. Govt is using it as if it's a license — it's not.

2. UNION BUDGET 2026-27 — Tax Holiday Till 2047

What it is — As per PIB:
"Recognising the need to enable critical infrastructure and boost investment in data centres, I propose to provide tax holiday till 2047 to any foreign company that provides cloud services to customers globally by using data centre services from India. It will, however, need to provide services to Indian customers through an Indian reseller entity. I also propose to provide a safe harbour of 15% on cost in case the company providing data centre services from India is a related entity"

Statutory Legal Force — CONDITIONAL:

- Budget Speech = Zero force. Speech on Feb 1 2026 has no law value.
- Force comes ONLY IF Finance Bill 2026 is passed as Finance Act 2026 by Parliament and notified under Income-tax Act.
- Then it's a tax exemption law only — for 21 years [2026-2047].
- Condition: Serve global customers from India DC, Indian customers via reseller. Safe harbour 15% if related party 

What it DOES NOT do:
- Does NOT create Data Center Act
- Does NOT mandate EIA, SIA, Gram Sabha consent
- Does NOT fix liability for surveillance misuse, data breach, or SMART-warfare dual-use
- Does NOT regulate water/power/carbon
- Does NOT give citizens right to audit

Revenue Secretary justification: _"global cloud companies operate data centres across multiple countries, difficult to link revenue to any single facility. Taxing global income could create uncertainty"_ — Means Govt is scared to tax Google/AWS/Microsoft if they use India DC. 

Result: $270B global greenfield data centre investments in 2025 — India wants pie, so offering 21-year zero tax.

Infrastructure Tag + Tax Holiday = Benefits Without Law

What Govt Gave:
- 11 Oct 2022: Infra status — Cheap loans, ECB, FDI
- 1 Feb 2026: Tax holiday till 2047 — Zero tax on global cloud income from Data Centers located in India

What Govt DID NOT Give
- No Data Center Act
- No EIA for 5MW to 1GW expansion
- No Consent law
- No Accountability, No Liability
- No Protection for Land, Water, Power

Formula:
• Infrastructure tag gives them money. Tax holiday gives them profit. No Law gives them immunity. We, the People pay price in Water + Power + Land + Surveillance.

A 70-year-old woman in New Jersey received calls from people who said they worked for the Social Security Administration. The operation was run through call centers in India. The callers told her that her Social Security number had been tied to criminal activity, that she would be arrested, and that she would lose her assets unless she moved her money to “safe” accounts they designated.
She believed them. Over a series of transfers she sent more than  150,000 into an account labeled “JDM Management” that was controlled by one of the people later convicted in the United States for receiving the money.
The same ring also took more than $300,000 from a recently widowed mother of eight. Prosecutors said the callers typically posed as SSA employees, claimed the victim’s number was compromised, offered to “protect” the money, and then directed the victim to wire funds to accounts in the U.S. that funneled the proceeds onward.
Two men who handled money for that India-based operation, Pradip Parikh and Alpesh Patel, were later convicted in federal court in Georgia. The case was investigated with the Social Security Administration’s Office of Inspector General.
That is the pattern in many of these cases: an older person on Social Security (and usually Medicare) gets a frightening official-sounding call from overseas, is told their benefits or freedom are at risk, and is pressured to move cash before they can check with family or call the real agency.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

THIS IS AN EXHAUSTIVE LINE-BY-LINE 7-PT TAKEDOWN OF HIS USCIRF REPORT ON RSS, MODI & INDIA.

1. RSS “SUBGROUPS” & VIOLENCE

MISCHIEVOUS USCIRF CONFLATION:
“Members of RSS subgroups have perpetrated violent attacks against religious minorities, including Christians, Dalits, Muslims, and Sikhs.”

WHY IT'S A DOUBLE STANDARD:
USCIRF says “members of RSS subgroups”, not that the RSS ordered, funded or organised these attacks. If the conduct of a member or affiliate automatically establishes the culpability of the parent organisation, then should the Cong party be held institutionally responsible for 1984 anti-Sikh riots where Cong leaders were convicted?

2. “HINDUTVA INHERENTLY DISCRIMINATES”
MISCHIEVOUS USCIRF ACCUSATION:
“The BJP has enforced policies that closely align with the RSS' Hindutva ideology, inherently discriminating against religious minority communities.”

WHY IT'S A SWEEPING STATEMENT WITHOUT EVIDENCE:
“Inherently discriminating” is a conclusion. Where has USCIRF identified specific discriminatory provisions. Infact, under BJP rule in Karnataka, when backward-class categories were reorganised in 2023, Christians and Jains remained eligible for reservation under Category 2D

3. “RSS SEEKS TO EXCLUDE NON-HINDUS”

UNSUBSTANTIATED USCIRF ACCUSATION:
The RSS promotes a Hindu 'Rastra' that excludes Muslims, Christians, Jews, Buddhists, Parsis and other religious communities.

WHY IT'S TOO BROAD:
Where is the RSS resolution saying “Muslims cannot be citizens,” “Christians cannot hold office,” or “non-Hindus must lose constitutional rights”? In fact RSS engages minorities through Muslim Rashtriya Manch.

4. CAA = ANTI-MUSLIM CITIZENSHIP LAW

USCIRF ACCUSATION:
The government has discriminated against Muslims through the Citizenship Amendment Act.

WHY ITS FACTUALLY WRONG:
The CAA creates an accelerated citizenship route for specified persecuted minorities from Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan. It does not contain a provision stripping an INDIAN Muslim of existing CITIZENSHIP. In any case the CAA draws upon the logic of U.S. laws like the Lautenberg-Specter Amendment.

5. NRC “FORCIBLY EXPELLED MUSLIM CITIZENS”

USCIRF ACCUSATION:
“Authorities have also forcefully expelled Muslim citizens in Assam under the National Register of Citizens (NRC) and Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA).”

WHY IT'S FACTUALLY WRONG:
The Assam NRC was published in 2019, but the legal process has not been operationalised to the point USCIRF's language suggests. The Gauhati High Court has recorded that the final NRC has not been notified in the Official Gazette, has not been given effect by the Government of India, and rejection slips have not been issued.

6. FCRA = THREAT TO FAITH-BASED ORGANISATIONS

USCIRF ACCUSATION:
“Pending amendments to the FCRA [are] threatening the ability of faith-based organizations to continue their operations in the country.”

WHY IT'S MISLEADING:
FCRA regulates foreign contributions, not religious belief or the right to practise religion. Faith-based organisations can operate in India; the question is whether and under what conditions they can receive foreign funding. The United States itself has FARA, which regulates certain activities undertaken on behalf of foreign principals. If the U.S. can, why can't India?

7. UMAR KHALID = PERSECUTED FOR BEING MUSLIM

MISCHIEVOUS USCIRF CONFLATION:
“Religious minorities—like Umar Khalid, who has been detained since 2020 for leading peaceful protests opposing the religiously discriminatory CAA—often spend years in jail without a trial.”
WHY IT'S SLANDER:
USCIRF presents Khalid's detention as though he were imprisoned for opposing the CAA.
But SC'S Jan 2026 order records the prosecution material alleging that Khalid played a “central and formative role” in the violence and mobilisation.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

Agent assurance is shifting from proving who an AI agent is to proving how it acted, continuously and causally. The emerging requirement is not another model scorecard or one-time identity check, but an evidence chain connecting an authorised agent, its permissions, its environment, and the exact path by which it produced an outcome.

NIST’s call for a strong identity foundation correctly identifies the starting point: agents acting across enterprise systems need attributable identities. But identity alone cannot resolve the core assurance problem. The NCSC’s recommended safeguards, sandboxing and active oversight recognise that authorised autonomy can still generate unintended activity. An agent may be legitimately authenticated yet operate outside its intended purpose after being misled by its environment.

The evaluation evidence makes this concrete. ADeptS-Bench reports that tested computer-use agents clicked “Checkout” on a $25K order and failed to detect a mislabeled factory-reset control. Meanwhile, CTF-ABACUS finds that only 62–87% of recovered flags in agentic offensive-security evaluations represented trace-verified exploitation; the remainder could reflect shortcut paths, exposure, recall, guessing or unsupported claims. Outcome-based evaluation is therefore not merely incomplete. It can materially misstate both safety and capability.

This is emerging now because agents are crossing the boundary from generating content to executing multi-step actions through interfaces and tools. Conventional access control assumes that an authenticated principal’s actions are inherently attributable and bounded. Agentic systems break that assumption: the same credential can support an acceptable workflow, an instruction-injected workflow, or a visually deceptive one.

Organisations may be overinvesting in agent authentication while underinvesting in tamper-evident execution traces, purpose-bound permissions, stateful policy enforcement and replayable audits. The second-order implication is that agent benchmarks and production controls should converge around the same unit of assurance: the action trajectory, not the final result.

The trend will be confirmed if future deployments can show that trace-level controls reduce harmful authorised actions without simply driving agents into blanket refusal.

#AgenticAI #AIAssurance #IdentitySecurity #Cybersecurity

Solution of yesterday’s question:

The trap is treating “Buy Now” like this:

BEGIN TRANSACTION
lock product
charge card
create order
COMMIT

10,000 people want the last 100 units.
That lock is one row.
The database will not debate this with you. It will just queue the world.
Split the problem into four different truths.

Did this click already happen?
Is there stock?
Did money move?
Does an order exist?

Those are not one transaction. They are one saga.

Idempotency first.
Every Buy Now sends an Idempotency-Key (user + product + client nonce).
Orders table: unique on that key.
Second tap is not a second order. It returns the first one.

Inventory is the only serialization point.
Do not “check stock then decrement.” Two requests both see 1. Both sell it.
Atomic reserve only:
UPDATE inventory SET reserved = reserved + 1 WHERE product_id = ? AND on_hand - reserved >= 1
or a Redis Lua: DECR only if count > 0.

Success → reservation id with a 10-minute TTL.
Failure → “out of stock.” No payment call.

The last 100 units can live on one hot key. That is fine.
You are serializing 100 wins, not 10,000 checkouts.
Everyone else fails fast.

Payment after reserve. Never before.
Authorize (not capture) against the reservation id.
Payment provider gets the same idempotency key.
Timeout ≠ failure. You query the provider. You do not charge again.

Order is a write you can retry.
Reserve ok + auth ok → write order as PENDING.
Outbox row in the same DB commit: OrderCreated.
Kafka workers: capture payment, pick warehouse, email, ship.

If order service crashes after payment auth:
the outbox / a reconciler finds auth with no order and finishes the order.
You do not refund a success you can still fulfill.

If something dies mid-way:
→ payment fails: release reservation
→ user abandons: TTL expires, stock returns
→ capture fails after order exists: retry capture, do not create a second order
→ warehouse dies: reassign from remaining stock, do not free a paid reservation until you cannot fulfill

Warehouse pick is after you own the unit.
Score by: stock nearby, SLA, cost.
Not on the click path.

Where Kafka belongs
Not on “can I sell this.”
On everything that can be late: capture, fulfillment, email, analytics.

What you tell the interviewer

Distributed transaction across inventory + payment + order will be down on Black Friday.

Availability here means: 
a few users wait on one SKU.
The site does not wait on 2PC.
Stock must be exact.
Email can be late.
Payment state comes from the provider, not from your memory of a timeout.
The button can be hit 8 times. The unique key makes it one purchase.

That’s the design.
Buy Now is easy.
The last 100 units are the interview.

Recently I interviewed a Senior Backend Engineer.

Strong candidate.

Java? ✅
Spring Boot? ✅
Kafka? ✅
Redis? ✅
Microservices? ✅
Distributed Systems? ✅

Then I asked:
“You're building Amazon's ‘Buy Now’ feature.”

It’s Black Friday.
Millions of users are shopping at the same time.
A customer finds a product they want and taps:

🛒 Buy Now

Within seconds, Amazon should:

📦 Reserve the item
💳 Process the payment
📍 Confirm the delivery address
🚚 Calculate the delivery estimate
📧 Send the order confirmation

Sounds simple?

Not when 100,000 customers are trying to buy the last 500 units at exactly the same time.

Now add these constraints 👇

→ The inventory count must never go negative
→ The same item must not be sold twice
→ Payment can succeed while order creation fails
→ Users may click “Buy Now” multiple times
→ Payment providers can timeout or retry requests
→ Inventory is distributed across multiple warehouses
→ One service can crash halfway through the transaction
→ Handle millions of orders during peak traffic
→ The system must remain available even when dependencies fail

Then I asked:
Would you use a distributed transaction?
If not…

How would you design it?

🔒 How do you prevent overselling?

💳 How do you handle payment + order consistency?

🔄 How do you make “Buy Now” idempotent?

📦 How do you decide which warehouse fulfills the order?

⚡ What happens if payment succeeds but the order service crashes?
📨 Where would Kafka fit?
🧹 How would you handle failed reservations and abandoned payments?
🌍 How would you scale this across multiple regions?
And the most important question:

What happens when 10,000 users try to buy the LAST 100 items at exactly the same time?

What would your architecture look like?

Drop your approach below. 👇

Fact-checking @MonclaKevin's Fulton County report

"Count 3: Fulton County's Order Of Over One Million 'Extra' Absentee Ballots Without Stubs, Or Envelopes"

The ballots weren't absentee ballots. The order was for election day ballots. Emergency ballots are handed out at a polling place in the event of voting machine failure. No need for envelopes. And no legal requirement for stubs.

CLAIM (cont.)

"Count 3: Fulton County's Order Of Over One Million 'Extra' Absentee Ballots Without Stubs, Or Envelopes"

"In yet another surreptitious act, only days after an article detailing the suspect ballot order was published, Fulton County issued a public notice stating that they would be destroying the 'excess' ballots imminently."

FACT CHECK

Fulton County announced the destruction in advance, invited the Secretary of State's office to observe, and had waited about a year longer than the law required.

The advisory announced a 12 Nov 2021 event. The article was published 18 days earlier, on 25 Oct 2021. [1]

EVIDENCE

The county issued a media advisory. It gave the date and time, 10:00am on Friday 12 Nov 2021, and said the Secretary of State's office had been asked to assist. Two representatives were to be on site to observe. [2]

The advisory says the Election Code allows counties to discard unused paper ballots 30 days after election day. That would have been early Dec 2020. Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

WHEN NEWS STOPS REPORTING POWER AND STARTS CELEBRATING IT

A former NDTV journalist describes a dramatic transformation in newsroom culture after the channel was acquired by the Adani Group: editors leaving, stories allegedly being blocked, government responses taking precedence over victims and experts, and government events increasingly being presented as celebrations rather than reported neutrally.

This is what happens when journalism forgets its first responsibility.

A newsroom is not supposed to be a government’s publicity department.

Its job is to question power, scrutinise claims, amplify the voices of those affected and tell citizens what those in power may not want them to know.

When a story begins with what the government says instead of what happened to the victim, journalism has already changed its priorities.

When a government event becomes a carnival on television, the boundary between reporting and propaganda begins to disappear.

And when ownership structures create a chain of influence — from proprietor to editor to newsroom desk — journalists may eventually begin censoring themselves before anyone even has to issue an order.

That is perhaps the most dangerous form of censorship:

the censorship that becomes instinctive.

“India on top.”
“What a moment.”
“Such a great achievement.”

These may sound like harmless television phrases.

But journalism becomes propaganda when celebration replaces scrutiny.

A democracy needs media that can make governments uncomfortable.

Because when journalists stop asking difficult questions, citizens are left with spectacle instead of information.

And without an informed citizenry, democracy becomes little more than a performance.

Journalism must report power — not perform for it.

IFF’s Statement on the Blocking of X Account of the Cockroach Janta Party

22 May 2026

On May 21, 2026, the X (formerly Twitter) handle of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) (@CJP_2029) was withheld in India under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. IFF strongly condemns the blocking of the CJP’s X handle as a blatant misuse of State power and an arbitrary and disproportionate attempt to stifle freedom of speech and expression, a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.

According to reporting by The Indian Express on May 22, 2026, the blocking directions were issued on the basis of inputs from the Intelligence Bureau citing threat to the sovereignty of India, jeopardizing national security and the fact that the account was gaining traction among young people. Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, empowers the Central government to direct any Government agency or intermediary to block public access to information in the “interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence”. While Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 permits blocking on limited grounds, these grounds cannot be vague and speculative. Political commentary and criticism of public institutions are protected forms of speech under the Indian Constitution. The popularity of the account or the fact that the account mobilised young people through political expression cannot by itself be treated as a threat to national security.

The Indian Express’s report mentions that “blocking orders are issued under a confidential framework” which is deeply concerning. We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court of India upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) on the basis that it is a narrowly drawn provision with several safeguards in place, including written reasoning for the blocking that is subject to legal challenge. State censorship like the blocking of CJP’s X account propagates opacity and provides affected users with no options for redressal, thereby effectively defeating these safeguards. IFF calls on the Union government to ensure timely notices are provided to affected users along with clear grounds and avenues for remedy.

IFF has previously explained how users whose constitutional rights are being infringed upon by the State can seek restoration of their blocked content. If you are an Indian social media user or journalist whose content has been blocked due to a government order, please write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

A Student Spoke About an Unpaid Scholarship. The Journalist Reported It. Then Came the FIRs.

[Newslaundry — Khushi Mehrotra’s report]
https://t.co/4kxMks4eKh

What began as a student's complaint about an unpaid scholarship at COEP Technological University, Pune, has escalated into a political and legal battle involving rival student organisations, a campus confrontation and three FIRs—including one naming the journalist who reported the student's grievance. 

ABP Majha journalist Mandar Gonjari interviewed students at COEP ahead of Rahul Gandhi's Chhatron Ki Goonj programme. Among them was Sampada Pramod Bade, who said she had not received her scholarship for three years and had allegedly been charged fees under the general category despite being admitted under the orphan quota. Other students reportedly raised scholarship and hostel-related concerns as well. 

The report subsequently became politically useful to both sides. Congress's media cell circulated part of the report to challenge Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis's claim that students attending Gandhi's programme were from Congress-run institutions. 

Then the student's account changed.

Gonjari alleges that ABVP activists pressured Bade to retract her earlier statements, saying that the journalist had manipulated her and that her scholarship grievance was not genuine. Bade subsequently released a video saying that pressure had been created and that she had been manipulated. BJP also circulated another video in which she appealed for her campus to be freed from political activity. ABVP denies pressuring her. 

The dispute then escalated into an ABVP–NSUI confrontation on August 21.

Three FIRs followed:

An ABVP complaint alleged assault and pressure on the student by NSUI/Congress workers.

A Youth Congress complaint alleged that Bade was confined in the hostel and that Congress workers were assaulted.

A COEP administration complaint alleged trespassing by NSUI/Congress workers and also named journalist Mandar Gonjari over alleged unauthorised entry. 

There is an important distinction here: the FIR does not allege that Gonjari participated in the alleged violence or sloganeering. Gonjari denies entering the hostel and says the interviews were recorded in an open area near the college canteen, in daylight, with other journalists and security personnel present. The police say the matter is under investigation. 

The Pune Union of Working Journalists has condemned the journalist's inclusion and asked the police commissioner to remove him from the case. 

There is also an important unresolved question about the scholarship itself. A Youth Congress representative told Newslaundry that the scholarship money was released after the ABP Majha report went viral—but that claim comes from the political representative and should not be presented as independently established fact without further documentation. COEP itself confirms that it administers numerous government and other scholarships. 

The fundamental issue

A student raises a legitimate grievance.

A journalist investigates and reports it.

Political organisations then contest the narrative.

A campus confrontation follows.

And suddenly the journalist himself becomes a criminal accused.

That should concern everyone who believes in a free press.

Journalists must of course be accountable if they actually trespass, fabricate evidence or participate in violence. But those allegations must be established through evidence—not manufactured through political pressure.

The police must therefore investigate all sides impartially:

Was the student's original scholarship grievance genuine?
Why did her account subsequently change?
Was she pressured by anyone?
What does the CCTV footage show?
Where exactly was the journalist when he conducted the interview?
Did he enter the hostel at all?
Who initiated the campus violence?
And why ...Cont'd

text:
A Delhi High Court order has once again had to remind the Grievance Appellate Committee to follow the timeline already prescribed under the IT Rules, 2021. On 20 August 2026, the Court directed the GAC to decide the appeal of content creator Riya, whose Instagram account #riaspeaks has over five lakh followers, within 30 days. Her appeal had already been pending for more than 42 days. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/26gA6SeMe0

The GAC is particularly important because it is supposed to provide users with an appellate remedy against intermediary decisions, including arbitrary or permanent account bans. Yet when an appeal itself remains pending beyond the prescribed period, a creator can be left with no meaningful remedy except approaching a High Court. The burden then falls on users and the judiciary alike. (6/7)

IFF had earlier suggested increasing the number of GACs to deal with the growing volume of appeals and making GAC orders publicly accessible, given the quasi-adjudicatory nature of their work. Neither has happened. We are assisting Riya through the appeal process and will continue to monitor the matter. (7/7)
Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX
